title: If two developers push at the same time, how does the pipeline handle it, and how do parallel/matrix builds work (e.g. GitHub Actions matrix)?
shortTitle: Concurrent Pushes and How Parallel and Matrix Builds Work

s1_definition.profdef: When two developers push concurrently, the version control system serialises the commits so each lands at a distinct point in history, and the CI system triggers a separate pipeline run per commit (or per branch). Those runs execute independently and in parallel on separate agents, each building its own commit. Shared stateful resources, such as a single deploy target or a limited license, are protected with concurrency controls so they are used by one run at a time. Parallel builds run independent steps of a single pipeline at the same time to cut wall-clock time, and a matrix build is a special form of parallelism that automatically expands one job definition across a set of parameter combinations, such as multiple Java versions or multiple services, running each combination as its own parallel job.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine two tellers at the National Bank of India each submitting a batch of cheques at the same moment. The clearing system does not get confused; it gives each batch its own serial number and processes them on separate machines at once, so neither waits for the other. But there is only one armoured van to the vault, so when it is time to physically deliver, the system makes them take turns with that one van. A matrix build is like testing a new cheque scanner against every combination of paper type and ink colour at once: instead of writing a separate test plan for each, you list "papers: A, B" and "inks: X, Y" and the system automatically runs all four combinations in parallel.
s1_definition.oneliner: Concurrent pushes get serialised into distinct commits and each runs its own pipeline in parallel, with concurrency locks guarding shared resources, while a matrix build auto-expands one job across many parameter combinations run in parallel.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When two developers push concurrently, the version control system serialises the commits so each lands at a distinct point in history, and the CI system triggers a separate pipeline run per commit (or per branch). Those runs execute independently and in parallel on separate agents, each building its own commit. Shared stateful resources, such as a single deploy target or a limited license, are protected with concurrency controls so they are used by one run at a time. Parallel builds run independent steps of a single pipeline at the same time to cut wall-clock time, and a matrix build is a special form of parallelism that automatically expands one job definition across a set of parameter combinations, such as multiple Java versions or multiple services, running each combination as its own parallel job.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine two tellers at the National Bank of India each submitting a batch of cheques at the same moment. The clearing system does not get confused; it gives each batch its own serial number and processes them on separate machines at once, so neither waits for the other. But there is only one armoured van to the vault, so when it is time to physically deliver, the system makes them take turns with that one van. A matrix build is like testing a new cheque scanner against every combination of paper type and ink colour at once: instead of writing a separate test plan for each, you list "papers: A, B" and "inks: X, Y" and the system automatically runs all four combinations in parallel.

**One line to remember:** Concurrent pushes get serialised into distinct commits and each runs its own pipeline in parallel, with concurrency locks guarding shared resources, while a matrix build auto-expands one job across many parameter combinations run in parallel.

sections.s2_technical:
Version control serialises the writes. Git on the server accepts pushes one at a time; if Rajesh and Priya push to the same branch simultaneously, one wins and the other is rejected with a non-fast-forward error and must pull and rebase, or if they push to different branches both succeed independently. Either way, every commit ends up at a unique position in history with a unique SHA, so there is never ambiguity about what each pipeline builds.

The CI system triggers one run per triggering event. A push to a branch, or an opened or updated pull request, starts its own pipeline run keyed to that exact commit SHA. Two concurrent pushes therefore produce two independent runs. On a Jenkins-on-Kubernetes or GitHub Actions setup, each run gets its own fresh agent (a pod or a runner), so they build in parallel with no shared workspace and cannot corrupt each other.

Shared stateful resources need explicit protection. The build and test phases are naturally isolated, but some things are singular: a single shared QA deploy slot, a limited number of software licenses, or an external system that cannot handle two simultaneous writers. For these you use a concurrency control. In GitHub Actions a `concurrency` group ensures only one run in that group proceeds at a time and can cancel superseded runs. In Jenkins you use the `lock` step from the Lockable Resources plugin, or `disableConcurrentBuilds`, to serialise access to the shared resource while leaving the rest parallel.

Parallelism inside one pipeline speeds up a single run. Independent stages, such as unit tests, integration tests, and a security scan, can run at the same time because they do not depend on each other's output. In a Jenkins Declarative pipeline you wrap them in a `parallel { }` block; in GitHub Actions you declare separate jobs that have no `needs` dependency so they run concurrently. The pipeline only proceeds past the parallel section when all branches finish, which is a fan-out then fan-in pattern.

A matrix build is parameterised parallelism. You declare a matrix of dimensions, and the CI system generates one job per combination automatically. In GitHub Actions this is `strategy: matrix:` with keys like `java: [17, 21]` and `service: [transfer, fraud]`, producing four jobs that run in parallel. This is how a banking platform verifies that every service compiles and passes tests on every supported JDK without hand-writing each job. Options like `fail-fast` control whether one failing combination cancels the rest, and `max-parallel` caps how many run at once to protect shared capacity.

A senior nuance is ordering and idempotency for deploys. Two concurrent merges to main could both try to deploy; the concurrency group should ensure the later commit wins and deploys last, so the environment ends on the newest code, not whichever finished first. Another nuance is cost and fairness: unbounded matrix expansion can swamp the runner fleet, so `max-parallel` and sensible matrix sizes matter on a shared banking CI system. A third nuance is flaky-test isolation: running tests in parallel can expose tests that share state (a static field, a fixed port, the same database row), which must be fixed to be independent or they will fail nondeterministically under parallelism.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh and Priya both pushed changes to the transfer service within the same second, and the old single-agent CI queued one behind the other, so the second change waited twenty minutes. Worse, an engineer once feared the two builds would "mix up." This is exactly the problem per-commit independent runs on separate agents solves. Each push becomes its own run on its own agent and they build in parallel with no interference.

Problem 2 — The pipeline ran unit tests, integration tests, and the security scan one after another, taking fifteen minutes even though they do not depend on each other. This is exactly the problem parallel stages solve. Running the three independently cuts the critical path to the slowest single stage.

Problem 3 — The platform supports two JDK versions and has many services, and the team hand-wrote a job per combination and kept forgetting some. This is exactly the problem a matrix build solves. One job definition expands across every JDK and service combination automatically.

Problem 4 — There is only one shared QA deploy slot, and two runs tried to deploy at once and clobbered each other. This is exactly the problem a concurrency lock solves. The shared QA slot is guarded so only one run deploys at a time.

To make this concrete without a CI server we will write a Java simulation. We will model concurrent pushes as two threads each running an independent `PipelineRun`, use a `parallel`-style executor to run independent stages at once within a run, expand a `MatrixBuild` across JDK and service combinations, and protect a shared QA deploy slot with a lock so concurrent runs serialise there. This mirrors real concurrent-push handling, parallel stages, matrix expansion, and resource locking.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two concurrent pushes (Rajesh's commit and Priya's commit) and a matrix of two JDKs by two services.

Step 1: Two threads start, one per commit, representing two independent CI runs on separate agents. They begin at the same time; neither waits for the other to start.

Step 2: Inside each run, three independent stages (unit tests, integration tests, security scan) are submitted to a small thread pool and run in parallel. The run waits for all three to finish, which is the fan-in, before moving on. The wall-clock time for this section is the slowest single stage, not the sum.

Step 3: Each run then reaches the shared QA deploy slot. The slot is protected by a fair lock, so only one run deploys at a time. Whichever run acquires the lock first deploys while the other waits, then the second deploys. The lock guarantees the single shared slot is never used by two runs at once, even though everything before it ran fully in parallel.

Step 4: After both runs finish, the matrix build runs. It expands the two JDKs crossed with the two services into four jobs and submits them to a pool capped at four parallel. Each of the four combinations builds and tests, and because max-parallel is four they all run at once.

Step 5: The output interleaves the two concurrent runs' parallel stages (so the line order varies), shows the QA deploys serialised one after the other, and shows the four matrix jobs. This demonstrates independence across runs, parallelism within a run, locking on a shared resource, and automatic matrix expansion.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh push (a1b2)        Priya push (c3d4)      ← serialised in Git, unique SHAs
       │                         │
       ▼                         ▼
  Run on agent A            Run on agent B          ← independent, parallel
       │                         │
   ┌───┼───┐                 ┌───┼───┐
   ▼   ▼   ▼                 ▼   ▼   ▼
  unit int scan             unit int scan           ← parallel stages (fan-out)
   └───┼───┘                 └───┼───┘
       ▼ (fan-in)                ▼ (fan-in)
       └──────────┬──────────────┘
                  ▼
         ┌──────────────────┐
         │ QA DeploySlot     │  ← single shared resource
         │ (fair lock)       │
         └──────────────────┘

  Matrix: {17,21} x {transfer,fraud} → 4 jobs run in parallel (max-parallel=4)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Parallel CI Classes ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Fan-out/Fan-in: invokeAll runs stages in parallel, join waits  │
  │  Lock/Guard: DeploySlot serialises access to a shared resource  │
  │  Parameterised expansion: MatrixBuild generates jobs per combo  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: PipelineRun runs one commit, DeploySlot guards one resource │
  │  O: new matrix dimension? add a loop, no run changes            │
  │  D: runs depend on DeploySlot abstraction for the shared slot   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     PipelineRun          │        │       DeploySlot         │
  │ - commit: String         │◇──────▶│ - lock: ReentrantLock    │
  │ - qaSlot: DeploySlot     │        │ + deploy(commit): void   │
  │ + run(): void            │        └──────────────────────────┘
  │ - runParallelStages()    │
  └──────────────────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     MatrixBuild          │
  │ + run(jdks, services,    │
  │       maxParallel)       │  one job per (jdk,service)
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Run Through Shared Slot ────────────────

  [RUNNING_PARALLEL_STAGES] → all done → [WAIT_FOR_QA_LOCK]
       │                                      │ lock acquired
       │                                      ▼
       │                              [DEPLOYING_QA] → release → [DONE]
       └── other run waits at WAIT_FOR_QA_LOCK until lock free

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. rajesh.start(); priya.start()
  2.   PipelineRun.run() → runParallelStages() (invokeAll fan-out/in)
  3.   → qaSlot.deploy(commit) → lock.lock() ... unlock()
  4. matrixBuild.run([17,21],[transfer,fraud],4) → 4 parallel jobs
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When two developers push at the same time, nothing gets mixed up because the layers each do their job. Git serialises the writes, so each push ends up at a unique position in history with its own commit SHA; if they push the same branch, one is accepted and the other must rebase, and if they push different branches both succeed. The CI system then triggers one independent pipeline run per triggering commit, and on a modern setup each run gets its own fresh agent, a Kubernetes pod or a hosted runner, so the two runs build their own commits fully in parallel with no shared workspace.

The only thing that needs care is shared stateful resources, like a single QA deploy slot or a limited license. The build and test phases are naturally isolated, but for a shared resource I add a concurrency control: a concurrency group in GitHub Actions, or a lock step in Jenkins, so only one run uses that resource at a time while everything else stays parallel.

Parallelism inside a single run speeds up the critical path. Independent stages such as unit tests, integration tests, and the security scan have no dependency on each other, so I run them together in a parallel block and the pipeline only continues once all of them finish. A matrix build is parameterised parallelism: I declare dimensions like java of 17 and 21 crossed with each service, and the CI system automatically generates one parallel job per combination, which is how I verify every service on every supported JDK without hand-writing each job. Options like fail-fast and max-parallel control whether one failure cancels the rest and how many jobs run at once.

On the banking project this mattered concretely. Concurrent pushes from Rajesh and Priya each ran on their own pod in parallel, the three test-and-scan stages ran in parallel to cut a fifteen-minute pipeline down to the slowest single stage, and a matrix covered both JDKs across all services so we never forgot a combination. A single shared QA slot was guarded by a lock so two runs could not clobber each other's deploy. The senior points I always add are that concurrent deploys to main must be ordered so the newest commit deploys last and the environment ends on the latest code, that I cap matrix expansion with max-parallel so a huge matrix does not swamp a shared CI fleet, and that parallel tests expose any test that secretly shares state, which has to be made independent or it fails nondeterministically.
